content: Seborrheic keratosis is a benign skin growth that is highly prevalent among individuals over the age of 40. The lesions associated with seborrheic keratosis often resemble flattened or raised warts. However, they are not caused by viral infections. These growths can present in a variety of colors, ranging from pink or yellow to shades of brown and black. Because they involve only the superficial layers of the epidermis, they are frequently described as having a pasted-on appearance. Treatment for seborrheic keratosis is generally unnecessary, as these growths are rarely painful. However, there is a minor risk of localized infection if the lesions are picked at. If a lesion becomes excessively itchy or is irritated by clothing or jewelry, cryosurgery has been shown to be an effective method for removal. The primary concern with seborrheic keratosis lies in its visual similarity to malignant melanomas, which can sometimes lead to a misdiagnosis of cancerous lesions. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty, a skin biopsy can provide definitive clarification and allow the physician to make an accurate diagnosis. A mutation in the gene encoding the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) has been implicated as a contributing factor in the development of seborrheic keratosis.
